p.src: Where there is something to tell, the tale is long; where there is nothing, it is brief. Now the vanguard of the great central column, under Guan Sheng, scouted straight to East New Bridge without seeing a single southern soldier. Suspicious, Guan Sheng withdrew beyond the bridge and sent a man back to report to Vanguard Commander Song. On hearing this, Song Jiang sent Dai Zong with an order: “For now, you must not advance rashly. Each day, two chieftains shall take turns scouting.” On the first day went Hua Rong and Qin Ming, and on the second Xu Ning and Hao Siwen; they scouted for several days running, yet still no enemy came out to fight. That day it was again the turn of Xu Ning and Hao Siwen. Taking several dozen horsemen, they scouted straight to the North Gate and found it standing wide open. As the two approached the drawbridge to look, a drum thundered atop the wall, and a body of troops burst from the city. As Xu Ning and Hao Siwen hurriedly wheeled their horses, shouts rose from a side road west of the city, and more than a hundred cavalrymen charged at their front. Xu Ning fought with all his strength and broke out through the cavalry, but when he looked back, Hao Siwen was nowhere to be seen. When he went back to look, he saw several officers seize Hao Siwen alive and carry him into the city. Just as Xu Ning hastened to turn back, an arrow struck him in the neck. He fled at full gallop with the arrow still lodged there, while six commanders pursued from behind. On the road he met Guan Sheng, who rescued him and brought him back, whereupon he collapsed unconscious from loss of blood. Guan Sheng had already driven back the six southern commanders, who returned to the city; word was hurriedly sent to Vanguard Commander Song. When Song Jiang hurried over to see Xu Ning, blood was flowing from all seven apertures of his head. Song Jiang shed tears and summoned the army physicians to treat him. They drew out the arrow and applied wound medicine. Song Jiang had him carried down into a warship to recuperate and personally came to tend him. He lost consciousness three or four times that night, and only then did they realize that the arrow had been poisoned. Song Jiang looked up to heaven and sighed: “‘Divine Physician’ An Daoquan has already been recalled to the capital, and there is no skilled doctor here who can save him. I am surely to lose one of my arms and legs!” His grief knew no bounds. Wu Yong came and urged Song Jiang to return to camp and deliberate on military affairs, lest affection for a brother cause him to neglect the weighty business of the state. Song Jiang had Xu Ning sent to Xiuzhou to recover, but the poison from the arrow proved incurable. Meanwhile, Song Jiang sent men among the troops to learn what had become of Hao Siwen. The next day, a soldier came to report: “On the wall above Hangzhou’s North Gate, they have hoisted Hao Siwen’s head on a bamboo pole for public display.” Only then did they learn that Fang Tianding had had him sliced to pieces. On receiving the news, Song Jiang was deeply grieved. Half a month later, an official dispatch arrived reporting that Xu Ning too had died. Having lost two commanders, Song Jiang held his troops in place and for the time being guarded the main road.

p.src: Now Li Jun and the others led their troops to encamp at North New Bridge, sending detachments as far as the deep mountains of Gutang to reconnoiter. Then came an urgent report: “Hao Siwen has been lost, and Xu Ning has died from an arrow wound.” Li Jun consulted Zhang Shun: “Considering this route of ours, the foremost concern is the strategic crossroads leading to Dusong Pass and to Huzhou and Deqing. Moreover, rebel troops roam everywhere here. If we block their vital thoroughfare, they will attack us from both sides, and with so few men we will be hard pressed to withstand them. We would do better to strike deep into the western hills and make camp there. The waters of West Lake would make a fine battlefield for us. Behind the western side of the hills lies a passage to Xixi, which would also furnish us a good line of retreat.” They immediately sent a junior officer to inform the vanguard commander and request his orders. Afterward they led their troops straight past Peach Spring Ridge into the depths of the western hills and encamped at the site of present-day Lingyin Temple; at the Xixi mountain pass north of the hills, in the depths of present-day Gutang, they also established a small stockade; while the vanguard came forward to Tangjiawa to scout. That day Zhang Shun said to Li Jun: “The southern troops have all withdrawn into Hangzhou. We have now been encamped here for half a month without seeing them come out to fight. If we do nothing but remain in the hills, when shall we ever win merit? Today I mean to swim underwater across the lake, slip secretly into the city through a water gate, and set a fire as our signal. Brother, you can then advance and seize their water gate, while reporting to our chief commander and vanguard so that all three columns attack the city together.” Li Jun said, “The plan is good, but I fear you cannot accomplish it alone.” Zhang Shun replied, “Even if I repay with this life the kindness our vanguard brother has shown me over so many years, it will be no great payment.” Li Jun said, “Wait a while before you go, brother. Let me first report to our elder brother and muster men to support you.” Zhang Shun said, “I shall set about my task here while you send someone to report. By the time I reach the city, our vanguard brother will already know.” That evening, Zhang Shun concealed a sharp knotweed-leaf dagger upon his person and ate and drank his fill. He came to the shore of West Lake and beheld green mountains on three sides and one lake of emerald water; in the distance stood the city walls, with four fortified gates facing the lakeshore. Those four gates were Qiantang Gate, Yongjin Gate, Qingbo Gate, and Qianhu Gate. Now, reader, be informed that before the former Song dynasty, Hangzhou was called Qinghe Town. In the time of King Qian, it was renamed the Ninghai Military Prefecture of Hangzhou, and ten city gates were established: in the east, Vegetable Market Gate and Jianqiao Gate; in the south, Houchao Gate and Jiahui Gate; in the west, Qianhu Gate, Qingbo Gate, Yongjin Gate, and Qiantang Gate; and in the north, North Gate and Genshan Gate. After Emperor Gaozong’s court crossed south, he established his capital here and called it the resplendent Lin’an Prefecture, adding three more city gates. At the time of Fang La’s occupation, however, it still had the form of King Qian’s old capital; its circuit measured eighty li. Though it could not compare in wealth and magnificence with the city as laid out after the southern crossing, its rivers and mountains had always been beautiful and its people luxurious; hence the saying passed down: “Above is Heaven; below are Suzhou and Hangzhou.” And how may this be seen?

p.src: Once the great metropolis of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, Qiantang has prospered since ancient times. Say nothing yet of the splendors within the city, but speak first of West Lake: ten thousand acres of pellucid blue shimmer like translucent glass, while three thousand green-clad peaks rise unevenly like ranks of jade. In the spring breeze upon the lake, radiant peach and luxuriant plum blossoms seem painted; in the summer ponds, green canopies and red lotuses resemble a picture; beneath autumn clouds reflected in the waters, tender southern chrysanthemums pile up gold; when winter snow flies, cold plum blossoms on the northern ridge burst like shattered jade. Along Nine-Li Pines, fine blue mist drifts; beneath the Six Bridges, emerald waters murmur clear and cold. Dawn’s rosy clouds shine across the Three Tianzhu Hills; evening clouds deeply enfold the Two Lofty Peaks. The wind rises where apes call at the cave mouth; rain sweeps over the summit of Dragon Well Hill. Beside the Hall of the Three Worthies, a dragon-back causeway soars toward heaven; before the Abbey of the Four Sages, a hundred fathoms of auspicious cloud coil and curl. Su’s Causeway preserves traces of Dongpo; the road by Solitary Hill passes He Jing’s former dwelling. Those visiting friends make for Lingyin; flower-decked revelers flock toward Jingci. In former days one heard only that the Three Isles lay afar; who knew that north of the lake was fairer than Penglai?

p.src: In the days of the former Song, the scenery of West Lake was indeed beyond compare and too splendid ever to describe in full. Zhang Shun came to Xiling Bridge and gazed upon it for a long while. It was the warmth of spring; the waters of West Lake stretched blue as indigo, while the surrounding hills rose in layer upon layer of emerald. After taking in the view, Zhang Shun said, “I was born and raised on the Xunyang River and have weathered countless fierce winds and towering waves, yet when have I ever seen such lovely waters as this lake? Even if I die here, I shall die a happy ghost!” With that, he took off his cloth shirt and left it beneath the bridge. His hair was gathered atop his head with a bright-red cord passed through the knot; around his waist he wore a raw-silk swimming skirt, with a shoulder sash tied about him and a sharp knife hanging from it. Then, barefoot, he plunged into the lake and felt his way across beneath the water. By then it was already the first watch, and the moon shone faintly. Zhang Shun felt his way close to Yongjin Gate and raised his head. Listening at the surface, he heard the watch drum upon the wall strike the fourth beat of the first watch. Outside the city all was utterly still, without a soul in sight; but beside the battlements atop the wall, four or five men were keeping watch. Zhang Shun submerged again and waited a while. When he next raised his head to look, not a single man could be seen by the battlements. He felt his way to the water gate and found its whole length barred by iron latticework; and when he reached inside, he found it protected throughout by water curtains, with cords attached to them and strings of bronze bells fastened to the cords. Seeing that the bars were solid and he could not enter the city, Zhang Shun thrust in one hand and tugged at a water curtain. This pulled the cord and set the bells ringing, and the men on the wall at once raised the alarm. Zhang Shun dove beneath the water and hid once more in the lake. He heard men and horses descending from the wall to inspect the water curtain. Finding no one there, they all said from atop the wall, “It is strange that the bells should ring. Perhaps some great fish swam down with the current and struck the water curtain.” The soldiers looked about for a while but saw nothing at all, so each went back to sleep. When Zhang Shun listened again, the tower had already sounded the third watch. After the watch beats had continued for some time, he reckoned that the soldiers must all have sprawled this way and that and fallen fast asleep. Zhang Shun dove toward the wall again, concluding that there was no way into the city through the water. He climbed ashore and looked up. Not a man was visible on the wall, and he was about to scale it when he reconsidered: “If anyone is still up there, I shall only throw my life away. Let me first put them to the test.” He gathered some clods of earth and tossed them onto the wall. Some soldiers who were still awake called the others up and went down once more to inspect the water gate, but again found nothing amiss. They then returned to the wall and looked out over the lake from the watchtower, but there was not a single boat upon it. It turned out that, by Fang Tianding’s command, all boats on West Lake had been brought into the waters outside Qingbo Gate and within Jingci Harbor; no boats were permitted to moor at any other gate. The men said, “What devilry can this be?” They said aloud, “It must be a ghost! Let us all go back to sleep and pay it no heed!” Yet though they said this, they did not go to sleep, but all lay hidden beside the battlements. Zhang Shun waited and listened through another watch. Hearing no movement, he swam close to the wall and listened again; the watch drum above had fallen silent. Still not daring to climb at once, Zhang Shun threw more earth and stones onto the wall, but again there was no response. Zhang Shun thought, “It is already the fourth watch and daybreak is near. If I do not scale the wall now, what further chance am I waiting for?” He had only just climbed halfway up the wall when a wooden clapper sounded above, and all the soldiers sprang up together. Zhang Shun leapt from halfway up the wall into the moat below and was about to escape beneath the water when treadle crossbows, powerful bows, bitter-bamboo arrows, and cobblestones all came shooting and pelting down from the wall at once. Alas for the hero Zhang Shun, who met his death in the moat outside Yongjin Gate! A poem says:

p.src: Now the tale divides in two. During the day, Song Jiang had received Li Jun's urgent report that Zhang Shun had dived beneath the water to enter the city, where he would set a fire as the signal, and that word had then been relayed to the troops at the eastern gate. That night, Song Jiang was discussing military affairs with Wu Yong in his tent. By the fourth watch he felt his mind grow weary, so he dismissed his attendants and lay down with his head resting on the table. Suddenly a blast of cold wind swept through. Song Jiang rose and looked about, only to see the lamplight dimmed and a bitter chill pressing in upon him. Peering intently, he saw something neither quite human nor quite a ghost, standing amid the icy air. When he looked at the figure, he saw that its whole body was stained with blood. In a low voice it said, “For many years I have followed you, elder brother, and deep indeed has been the affection between us. Now I have repaid you with my life and died amid the spears and arrows beneath Yongjin Gate. I have come especially to bid you farewell.” Song Jiang cried, “Why, is that not my brother Zhang Shun!” Turning his face the other way, he saw three or four more figures, all drenched in fresh blood, though he could not make them out clearly. Song Jiang gave a great wail and abruptly awoke: it had been no more than a dream beneath the southern bough. Hearing the cry, the attendants outside the tent came in to see what was wrong. Song Jiang exclaimed, “How strange!” He ordered them to summon the military adviser to interpret his dream. Wu Yong said, “You were overcome by weariness for only a short while, elder brother. What strange dream did you have?” Song Jiang replied, “Just now, as a chill swept past, I saw Zhang Shun as plainly as could be, his whole body stained with blood. He stood right here and told me, ‘For many years I have followed you, elder brother, and the kindness you have shown me has been boundless. Now I have repaid you with my life and died amid the spears and arrows beneath Yongjin Gate. I have come especially to bid you farewell.’ When I turned my head, three or four other bloodstained men were standing on this side. I could not see them clearly, and then I awoke weeping.” Wu Yong said, “Li Jun reported this morning that Zhang Shun intended to cross the lake, scale the city wall, and set a fire as a signal. Could it be that the matter remained in your thoughts, elder brother, and so gave rise to this ominous dream?” Song Jiang said, “I cannot help thinking that Zhang Shun, quick and resourceful though he is, must surely have met an undeserved death.” Wu Yong said, “The approaches from West Lake to the city must be narrow and perilous. I fear he truly has lost his life. Zhang Shun's spirit must have come to you in a dream.” Song Jiang asked, “If that is so, then who were those other three or four men?” He and Scholar Wu debated the matter without reaching any conclusion. They sat waiting for dawn, but no movement at all came from within the city, and Song Jiang's suspicions only deepened. Toward the afternoon, a messenger sent by Li Jun came racing in with this report: “Zhang Shun tried to scale the wall at Yongjin Gate, but was shot with arrows and died in the water. At this very moment, on the wall beside West Lake, they have mounted his head on a bamboo pole and hung it up as a warning.” On receiving the report, Song Jiang wept until he fainted. Wu Yong and all the other commanders were likewise overcome with grief. For Zhang Shun had been a man of excellent character and had won the deep affection of all his brothers. Song Jiang said, “Even when I lost my parents, I did not grieve as I do now. I cannot keep this pain from piercing my very heart and bones!” Wu Yong and the assembled commanders urged him, “Elder brother, keep the affairs of the realm foremost in your mind. Do not injure your honored person out of brotherly grief.” Song Jiang said, “I must go to the lakeside in person and mourn for him.” Wu Yong remonstrated, “You must not personally venture into so dangerous a place, elder brother. If the enemy learns of it, they will certainly come to attack you.” Song Jiang replied, “I have a plan of my own.” He immediately selected Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun, and sent them ahead with five hundred infantrymen to scout the road. Song Jiang followed with Shi Xiu, Dai Zong, Fan Rui, and Ma Lin, leading another five hundred soldiers secretly along a narrow path through the western hills to Li Jun's encampment. u.src: Now the tale divides in two. During the day, Song Jiang had received Li Jun's urgent report that Zhang Shun had dived beneath the water to enter the city, where he would set a fire as the signal, and that word had then been relayed to the troops at the eastern gate.

That night, Song Jiang was discussing military affairs with Wu Yong in his tent. By the fourth watch he felt his mind grow weary, so he dismissed his attendants and lay down with his head resting on the table.
Suddenly a blast of cold wind swept through. Song Jiang rose and looked about, only to see the lamplight dimmed and a bitter chill pressing in upon him.
Peering intently, he saw something neither quite human nor quite a ghost, standing amid the icy air.

When he looked at the figure, he saw that its whole body was stained with blood. In a low voice it said, “For many years I have followed you, elder brother, and deep indeed has been the affection between us.
Now I have repaid you with my life and died amid the spears and arrows beneath Yongjin Gate. I have come especially to bid you farewell.”
Song Jiang cried, “Why, is that not my brother Zhang Shun!”
Turning his face the other way, he saw three or four more figures, all drenched in fresh blood, though he could not make them out clearly.
Song Jiang gave a great wail and abruptly awoke: it had been no more than a dream beneath the southern bough.
Hearing the cry, the attendants outside the tent came in to see what was wrong. Song Jiang exclaimed, “How strange!”
He ordered them to summon the military adviser to interpret his dream.
Wu Yong said, “You were overcome by weariness for only a short while, elder brother. What strange dream did you have?”

Song Jiang replied, “Just now, as a chill swept past, I saw Zhang Shun as plainly as could be, his whole body stained with blood. He stood right here and told me, ‘For many years I have followed you, elder brother, and the kindness you have shown me has been boundless.
Now I have repaid you with my life and died amid the spears and arrows beneath Yongjin Gate. I have come especially to bid you farewell.’
When I turned my head, three or four other bloodstained men were standing on this side. I could not see them clearly, and then I awoke weeping.”

Wu Yong said, “Li Jun reported this morning that Zhang Shun intended to cross the lake, scale the city wall, and set a fire as a signal. Could it be that the matter remained in your thoughts, elder brother, and so gave rise to this ominous dream?”
Song Jiang said, “I cannot help thinking that Zhang Shun, quick and resourceful though he is, must surely have met an undeserved death.”
Wu Yong said, “The approaches from West Lake to the city must be narrow and perilous. I fear he truly has lost his life.
Zhang Shun's spirit must have come to you in a dream.”
Song Jiang asked, “If that is so, then who were those other three or four men?”
He and Scholar Wu debated the matter without reaching any conclusion. They sat waiting for dawn, but no movement at all came from within the city, and Song Jiang's suspicions only deepened.

Toward the afternoon, a messenger sent by Li Jun came racing in with this report: “Zhang Shun tried to scale the wall at Yongjin Gate, but was shot with arrows and died in the water. At this very moment, on the wall beside West Lake, they have mounted his head on a bamboo pole and hung it up as a warning.”
On receiving the report, Song Jiang wept until he fainted.
Wu Yong and all the other commanders were likewise overcome with grief.
For Zhang Shun had been a man of excellent character and had won the deep affection of all his brothers.
Song Jiang said, “Even when I lost my parents, I did not grieve as I do now. I cannot keep this pain from piercing my very heart and bones!”
Wu Yong and the assembled commanders urged him, “Elder brother, keep the affairs of the realm foremost in your mind. Do not injure your honored person out of brotherly grief.”
Song Jiang said, “I must go to the lakeside in person and mourn for him.”
Wu Yong remonstrated, “You must not personally venture into so dangerous a place, elder brother. If the enemy learns of it, they will certainly come to attack you.”
Song Jiang replied, “I have a plan of my own.”

He immediately selected Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun, and sent them ahead with five hundred infantrymen to scout the road. Song Jiang followed with Shi Xiu, Dai Zong, Fan Rui, and Ma Lin, leading another five hundred soldiers secretly along a narrow path through the western hills to Li Jun's encampment.
Li Jun and the others received him and escorted him to rest in the abbot's quarters at Lingyin Temple.
Song Jiang wept once more, then asked the monks of the temple to chant sutras there and perform rites for the repose of Zhang Shun's soul.

u.src: At dusk the following day, Song Jiang ordered a soldier to raise a white mourning banner by the lakeside, upon which were written the words: “To the spirit of my departed brother, Commander Zhang Shun.

p.src: The banner was planted at the water's edge. Many sacrificial offerings were arranged upon Xiling Bridge, and then Song Jiang gave Li Kui secret instructions as to what he must do. Li Kui was to lie in ambush at the entrance to the northern mountain road. Fan Rui, Ma Lin, and Shi Xiu were to lie in ambush on either side. Dai Zong was to remain at Song Jiang's side. They waited until nightfall, near the first watch. Song Jiang then donned a white robe and covered his golden helmet with a layer of mourning silk. Accompanied by Dai Zong and five or seven monks, he went around Xiaoxing Hill and came onto Xiling Bridge. The officers had already set out black pigs, white sheep, and offerings of gold and silver. They lit candles until all shone brilliantly and kindled incense. Song Jiang presided over the rite at the center, facing Yongjin Gate as he wept and poured libations. Dai Zong stood at his side. First the monks rang their bells and chanted incantations, summoning the spirit by name and invoking Zhang Shun, that his soul might descend and alight upon the spirit banner. Next Dai Zong read aloud the funeral oration. Song Jiang personally poured out the wine as a libation, then raised his face to heaven, looked eastward, and wept. In the midst of his lamentation, shouts suddenly arose from both ends beneath the bridge, while drums thundered together from the northern and southern hills: two columns of troops were charging in to seize Song Jiang. All because his loyalty and brotherly love were vast as heaven, the clash of arms now swept across the earth. How Song Jiang and Dai Zong met the enemy will be revealed in the next chapter.
